content: The Cystic Fibrosis Foundation (CFF) is a non-profit organization based in the United States that was created with the goal of curing and managing cystic fibrosis (CF). The Foundation provides comprehensive information about cystic fibrosis and funds research aimed at improving the quality of life for individuals living with the disease. Additionally, the Foundation actively participates in legislative advocacy efforts to support the needs of the CF community. The Cystic Fibrosis Foundation was founded in 1955 by a group of volunteers in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. Since its inception, the Foundation has provided grants to support research into cystic fibrosis and has facilitated clinical trials to advance treatment options. It also accredits and promotes 115 specialized care centers across the United States that are dedicated to treating individuals with CF. The Foundation operates through more than 80 chapters and offices nationwide. A significant milestone in its history occurred in 1989 when scientists funded by the Foundation identified the gene responsible for cystic fibrosis, a discovery that has been pivotal in the pursuit of a cure. The Foundation has also been instrumental in the development of four FDA-approved therapies for CF, underscoring its leadership in advancing treatment for the disease. The term 65 Roses® is a registered trademark popularized by the Cystic Fibrosis Foundation in the United States. This term serves as a simpler alternative to the often challenging pronunciation of cystic fibrosis. According to the Foundation's history, the phrase originated in 1965 when a volunteer named Mary Weiss heard her four-year-old son, Richard Weiss, pronounce cystic fibrosis as 65 Roses. Since then, the term has been embraced by children with the disease and has become closely associated with the Foundation. The rose has also been adopted as a symbol of the Foundation, further reinforcing the connection between the term and its mission.
